newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's apartheid generals acquitted of murder.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's apartheid generals acquitted of murder.

text.p: Former South African defence minister Magnus Malan, who led the "dirty war" to preserve apartheid, was acquitted on Friday of ordering the massacre of 13 blacks.

Malan, the most senior apartheid-era leader to be tried for atrocities against the black majority, was found not guilty of masterminding the 1987 death squad murders in KwaMakhuta near the Indian Ocean port city of Durban.
Three generals, a vice-admiral, a brigadier, a major and a top official of the Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party were also acquitted.
In a statement immediately after his acquittal Malan thanked President Nelson Mandela for allowing the accused to defend themselves in a court of law and called the outcome a "victory of justice".

The not guilty verdict was expected to anger anti-apartheid activists who bore the brunt of Malan's military force during their fight against white domination and remain convinced that death squads were sanctioned at the very top.
But political analysts said they were not suprised by Friday's outcome, since the prosecution's case appeared shaky from the outset.

Judge Jan Hugo, who dismissed all charges against Malan and 15 co-defendants, said the prosection's case was fundamentally flawed. He exonerated the former defence minister of all charges including murder, attempted murder and conspiracy to murder.
"We have found no proof of express authorisation of the KwaMakutha incident...or tacit approval (by the military),'' Hugo told the court.
South Africa does not operate a jury system. Rulings are made by a judge in consultation with two assessors.

The state had tried to show the accused organised the attack as part of a covert defence force operation using the mainly Zulu-based Inkatha Freedom Party against Mandela's then-banned African National Congress.
Judge Hugo said much of the documentary evidence dealt with a paramilitary force set up under Malan to help Inkatha leader Mangosuthu Buthelezi.
He said the documents presented in the case did not imply that this meant a death squad, adding that crucial to the state's case was the term "offensive" unit, found in many of the documents.
It often seemed to have an "innocent" meaning, in that it did not mean death squads, but a security function, he added.

Malan apparently expected acquittal. He turned up in court on Friday, the final day of a seven-month trial, waving and giving a thumbs-up sign to crowds gathered outside the colonial-style courthouse.
The prosecution's case began to crumble visibly on Thursday when six policemen were cleared of carrying out the attack.
Inkatha hailed Thursday's acquittal as "a triumph of justice".
"The state should in future be more prudent and cautious before embarking on prosecutions which are widely perceived to have high-level political connotations," it said in a statement.
Mandela's ruling African National Congress had no immediate comment on Malan's acquittal but called Thursday's verdict a travesty.

"In the eyes of our people, the prosecution team failed them. This will have far reaching consequences. It is doubtful whether our people will ever have confidence in the judicial system if it remains the same," the ANC said.
"This could lead to a ratcheting up of tensions between the ANC and the IFP in Natal," said political analyst Tom Lodge of the University of the Witwatersrand.
But he said he was not suprised Malan and the others had been acquitted, because "at no stage did the evidence indicate a chain of command, everything was hearsay".
"I think people like Malan knew and encourages such activities, but you have to prove it," Lodge told Reuters.

Senior members of the ANC have lamented the fact that most of South Africa's judges are white men appointed during the apartheid era, and have accused some of them of administering racially-biased justice in the past.
